name: Pore vacuum

card.summary: A handheld suction gadget sold to pull blackheads from pores; no clinical trials back or refute it.
card.note: Skin trauma and bruising are risks of any aggressive extraction; no trials exist.

quick.overview:
A pore vacuum is a small electric suction tool that is pressed on the skin to pull out blackheads and surface oil. It is a popular consumer skin-care gadget.

No published clinical trials of these devices were found, so the evidence for their effect is limited to manufacturer claims and user anecdotes.
quick.mechanism: The device creates suction at a nozzle placed against the skin. The intent is to draw keratin and sebum out of open comedones. Dermatology references describe manual extraction and retinoids as established approaches to comedones.
quick.risks: General guidance on extraction notes risks of irritation, infection and scarring from skin trauma. No safety studies of consumer suction devices were found.

lead: A pore vacuum, also sold as a blackhead vacuum or electric pore extractor, is a handheld device that applies adjustable suction through a small nozzle held against the skin. People use it on the nose and cheeks to draw out blackheads and oil, aiming for clearer-looking pores and smoother skin texture [2].

Blackheads are open comedones, hair follicles blocked by keratin and sebum whose dark surface comes from oxidation rather than dirt [1]. Grokipedia describes the devices as home versions of professional pore-suction tools, usually used after steaming or a warm compress and followed by moisturiser, with interchangeable tips and several suction levels [2]. Dermatologists cited there describe results as temporary since pores can refill, and prefer salicylic acid or retinoids for ongoing pore care [2].
No published clinical trial of consumer pore vacuums was identified, so what is known comes from manufacturers, dermatology commentary and user reports.

chain: Suction lifts sebum and keratin plugs from open pores
Visible blackheads on nose and cheeks are reduced
angle.text: Users run the device over the nose and cheeks to pull out visible blackheads, which makes pores look cleaner for a while. Results are described as temporary, so people repeat it periodically.

infobox: Interchangeable nozzles, several suction levels, rechargeable battery
Sold as a consumer cosmetic device; not described as an FDA-regulated medical device [2]

paras: Consumer pore vacuums are small electric units with a vacuum pump and nozzle heads of different shapes and openings. The user presses the nozzle to the skin and moves it across the area, typically after steaming or washing with warm water to soften the plugs [2]. Some models add exfoliating heads, LED light or serum infusion [2].

Comedones form when keratin and sebum block a follicle. An open comedone is a blackhead and a closed one is a whitehead. Wikipedia lists contributors such as increased oil production, genetics, greasy hair products and ingrown hairs, and notes that excess washing or scrubbing can irritate skin [1].

Dermatologists can often remove open comedones with minimal trauma, comedo extractors are used with careful hygiene after steaming or warm washing, and squeezing can cause infection or scarring [1]. Retinoids and azelaic acid are described as beneficial treatments, and pore-cleansing strips as potentially damaging [1]. The Wikipedia article does not address suction devices.

Grokipedia says suction mainly removes superficial contents and works best on pre-softened skin rather than deeply embedded comedones [2]. It says dermatologists caution that holding the device in one spot, using high suction or using it too often can cause bruising, redness, broken capillaries or micro-tears, particularly on sensitive, rosacea-prone or hyperpigmentation-prone skin, and that experts suggest low suction, continuous movement and occasional use [2]. Grokipedia is AI-generated, so these points reflect that source's summary of dermatologist commentary.
